lesson.title: Does Everyone Smile the Same Way? Universal Basic Emotions
lesson.summary: Paul Ekman's research proposed that a small set of basic emotions, happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust, produce facial expressions that people across cultures can recognize, though how truly universal this is remains an active scientific debate.
lesson.body:
One of the deepest questions running through the theories of emotion is whether emotion is fundamentally a built-in biological program, shared across humanity because it evolved before culture existed, or whether it is something culture and language construct and shape from the ground up. The universal basic emotions claim is the strongest version of the biological-program side of that argument, and it comes from a specific, influential body of research.

Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen conducted fieldwork in the late 1960s with the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, a group that at the time had very little exposure to Western media, faces, or customs. Ekman showed Fore participants photographs of Western facial expressions paired with short stories describing emotional situations, and separately asked Fore participants to pose the facial expression that would fit a given story. When these Fore expressions were later shown to Western viewers unfamiliar with the culture, recognition was well above what chance guessing would predict. From this and related work, Ekman proposed six basic emotions with reliably recognizable facial expressions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust.

This finding was influential, but it is important to represent the state of the science honestly: it is genuinely contested, not settled. Later cross-cultural studies found that recognition accuracy, while consistently above chance, is far from perfect and varies noticeably across emotions and cultures. Researchers also documented an in-group advantage, meaning people tend to be somewhat more accurate at reading emotional expressions from members of their own cultural group than from unfamiliar ones. Some emotions, like happiness and disgust, tend to be recognized more reliably across cultures than others, like fear and surprise, which are sometimes confused for each other. Critics, including researchers such as Lisa Feldman Barrett, have argued more broadly that facial expressions are more variable, more dependent on context, and more actively constructed by the perceiver than a strict universal-signal model suggests, and meta-analyses of the evidence have found considerable inconsistency across studies.

A reasonable middle position, and the one many psychologists currently hold, is that some biological substrate for a handful of core expressions likely exists (evidence such as similar expressions of triumph and defeat in athletes who have been blind since birth, and who therefore could never have learned these expressions by watching others, is often cited in support of this), while culture substantially shapes how strongly, how often, and in what circumstances people display and interpret those expressions. That cultural shaping is exactly what the next chapter, on display rules for emotion, examines directly.
